metadata.title: Learners for Life: Student Approaches to Learning (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The report uses PISA 2000 nationally representative samples of 15-year-olds in participating countries, with generalization intended to the target population of 15-year-olds in each country. For school-level questionnaire responses, the report states that principal responses are weighted to be proportionate to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in the school. For student-level analyses, the excerpt does not specify the exact student sampling weight variable(s) or whether replicate weights were used, so the weighting strategy cannot be fully reconstructed from the provided text. The analysis also relies on PISA’s standardized scaling of learner-characteristic scales (1–4 mean scores) and on cross-country comparability checks; however, no explicit plausible-values or missing-data handling procedures are described in the excerpt.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This report is primarily descriptive and correlational about students’ self-reported approaches to learning (motivation, self-related beliefs, learning strategies, and learning preferences), rather than an empirical ML prediction of cognitive achievement using PISA plausible values. The excerpt does not document a specific plausible-values procedure for the learner-characteristic outcomes, and it does not provide a missing-data handling protocol for the questionnaire-based scales. Therefore, plausible-values handling and missing-data handling are not reported in a way that can be mapped to PV-based achievement analysis conventions.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report analyzes PISA 2000 student approaches to learning questionnaire data administered in 26 countries (22 OECD and 4 non-OECD). The excerpt specifies that 120,740 students participated in the self-regulated learning questionnaire, and it notes that only the Flemish part of Belgium and only Scotland in the United Kingdom participated in this part of the survey. Beyond this, the excerpt does not specify additional analytic exclusions (e.g., missing questionnaire items, response-rate thresholds beyond notes about comparability, or specific sub-samples for particular chapters).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report uses PISA 2000 to study how students’ self-reported approaches to learning—motivation, self-related beliefs (self-efficacy and self-concept), learning strategies (memorisation, elaboration, and control strategies), and preferences for cooperative/competitive learning—relate to reading literacy performance. The report draws on a dedicated self-regulated learning questionnaire completed by 15-year-olds in 26 countries (120,740 students), and it combines these learner-characteristic scales with PISA reading literacy results to examine within-country associations, cross-country comparability, and subgroup differences (e.g., gender, socio-economic status, immigrant status, and strong vs weak readers). Key quantitative summaries include performance gaps between top and bottom quarters on learner scales (often around 30–100 reading literacy points) and variance-explained statements (e.g., about one-fifth of reading literacy variance explained by approaches to learning; about two-thirds of variance in control strategies explained by motivation and self-related beliefs). The report also uses clustering to identify student profiles with generally strong vs weak approaches, and it emphasizes that self-reports may not be directly comparable across cultures for some scales. No machine-learning model training or predictive algorithm evaluation is described in the provided text.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse with respect to ML methodology because this is an OECD descriptive/cross-national analysis report rather than an empirical machine-learning study. The excerpt does not provide per-country analytic Ns, explicit missing-data handling, or any PV-handling procedure for learner-characteristic outcomes, and it does not describe training/evaluation of ML algorithms. Therefore, ML-specific fields are left empty and the findings are summarized at the level of PISA scale relationships and policy implications rather than predictive model performance.
